readerTitle: The budget said no while customers were calling
caseNote: 가상 사례 (배관·난방 서비스 회사, B2B 마케팅 대행사) + 실제 기업 (Handelsbanken의 연간 예산 폐지). 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 연간 예산은 1년에 한 번 찍은 사진이다. 상황이 바뀌면 목표는 그대로 두고, 앞으로 12개월 전망과 돈 쓰는 결정을 다시 맞춘다.
misconception: 한 번 정한 연간 예산을 끝까지 지키는 것이 재무 규율이다. 예산보다 덜 쓰면 무조건 잘한 것이다.

sources.text: Wallander, J. (1999). Budgeting — an unnecessary evil. Scandinavian Journal of Management, 15(4).
Hope, J. & Fraser, R. (2003). Beyond Budgeting. Harvard Business School Press.
배관·난방 회사와 마케팅 대행사 사례, 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Handelsbanken이 1970년대 Jan Wallander CEO 시절 전통적 연간 예산을 폐지했다는 내용은 Wallander(1999)와 Hope & Fraser(2003)에 나옵니다. 정확한 연도(1970년대 초)와 현재도 같은 방식인지 게시 전 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 연도 없이 'in the 1970s'로만 적었습니다.
Beyond Budgeting Round Table이 Handelsbanken 등의 사례에서 영감을 받았다는 서술은 Hope & Fraser(2003) 기준입니다. 확인 필요.
가상 수치 계산: 연 매출 계획 $2.4M, 4월까지 실적이 계획보다 25% 높음(설명용). 차트의 '남은 전망 기간'은 1월 12개월, 4월 9개월, 7월 6개월, 10월 3개월. 대행사 사례: 최대 고객이 매출의 30%라는 가정.

cards.title: The budget said no while customers were calling
body: A heating and plumbing company sets its budget every October: revenue, ad spend, and two new technicians next spring.
Then a cold February hits. Pipes burst across town. By April, revenue is running 25% above plan. The budget still says two hires and not a dollar more on ads.

image.label: Ringing phone next to a locked budget binder
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작업용 밴 옆 사무실 책상 위에 계속 울리는 전화기와 자물쇠가 채워진 'Budget 2025' 바인더. 창밖에는 눈과 얼어붙은 파이프. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: Demand is up. The budget hasn't moved.
body: Your service manager wants a third new technician and more ads now. Customers are waiting ten days for a visit. The annual budget doesn't allow either.

options.text: Stick to the budget. Discipline matters, and spring may slow down
options.feedback: You protect the plan, but the plan was built on last October's guesses. Waiting customers may call a competitor and not come back.

options.text: Approve the hire and ads. Revenue is up, so you can afford it
options.feedback: Right instinct to respond, but you're reacting to one strong quarter. A hire is a year-long cost, so check whether demand is likely to hold.

options.text: Re-forecast the next 12 months, then fund the hire if demand still holds
options.feedback: You act on fresh information without betting on one cold snap. That's the idea in this lesson.

cards.title: The budget looked great. The business didn't.
body: The owner held the line. Spending came in right on budget, and the monthly report showed costs under control.
But wait times stretched to two weeks. Some customers booked rival firms, and a few of those became their regular plumber. By autumn, the extra demand had faded, partly because it went elsewhere.
The budget did its job: it limited spending. It just answered the wrong question.

image.label: Report with green checkmarks beside an empty appointment book
image.brief: 왼쪽은 초록 체크 표시가 가득한 예산 보고서, 오른쪽은 가을 들어 빈칸이 많아진 예약 달력. 두 화면의 대비가 핵심.

cards.title: A fixed budget sees less and less ahead.
body: A January budget looks 12 months ahead. By October it only sees to December. A rolling forecast always looks the same distance forward.

image.label: Fixed budget horizon shrinks, rolling stays 12 months

cards.title: Fixed budgets vs rolling forecasts
body: A **fixed budget** is set once for the year and used to judge results. A **rolling forecast** is updated on a schedule, often every quarter, and always looks the same distance ahead, such as the next 12 months.
The deeper shift: keep three things apart. The *target* is what you aim for. The *forecast* is what you honestly expect. *Spending decisions* follow the latest forecast, not last year's guess.
cards.softwareNote: Cloud and support costs often grow with usage. An annual server budget can be out of date within weeks, so many software teams tie spending to a rolling forecast of active users.

cards.title: A bank that dropped the annual budget.
body: In the 1970s, the Swedish bank Handelsbanken stopped using traditional annual budgets, a change led by its then-CEO Jan Wallander. He argued that budgets either repeat what everyone already knows or guess wrong about what nobody knows.
The bank judged branches against each other and against past results instead. Its approach later inspired the *Beyond Budgeting* movement.

image.label: Old annual plan torn, replaced by a moving 12-month window
image.brief: 반쯤 찢긴 연간 달력 종이 옆에, 앞으로 계속 미끄러지는 12칸짜리 투명 창(슬라이딩 윈도). 은행 건물은 일반적 형태로, 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Rolling forecasts aren't free.
body: Updating a forecast takes hours every quarter. Update monthly in a stable business and you mostly produce noise.
If the forecast also becomes the target, people lowball it to look good later. Keep the target separate.
And some limits should stay fixed: a minimum cash balance, a grant's spending rules, a client contract's price. In a steady business, a simple fixed budget may be all you need.

cards.title: Now it's a marketing agency.
body: Your 25-person agency loses its biggest client in May. That client was 30% of revenue. Every team still has its full annual budget approved.

options.text: Keep the budget. New clients may make up the gap by December
options.feedback: You avoid a painful meeting, but you keep spending as if 30% of revenue still exists. Hope isn't a forecast.

options.text: Cut every team's budget by 30% right away
options.feedback: Fast and fair-looking, but it cuts the work that wins new clients as deeply as the work that served the lost one.

options.text: Re-forecast the next 12 months without the client, then decide which spending still pays off
options.feedback: You face the new reality and still choose where to cut. It takes a few days, but each dollar gets a fresh decision.

cards.title: Keep the target. Update the view.
body: A budget is a snapshot of what you believed once. When the world moves, re-forecast the next 12 months and let spending follow.
**Try it today:** take your current budget and write a fresh forecast for the next four quarters. Circle the biggest gap between the two.
